Probability Calculator

Compute a binomial probability for exactly, at most, or at least k successes in n independent trials with the same success probability. It also reports the expected number of successes, so the event probability has useful context. For X~Binomial(n,p), P(X=k)=C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k). Cumulative options sum the relevant outcomes from 0 through n. “At most k” includes zero through k; “at least k” includes k through n. The model describes a fixed number of independent trials with one shared success chance, such as repeated draws with replacement or repeated fair coin flips.

How to use this calculator

  1. Enter number of trials, success count or threshold, success probability and the remaining inputs.
  2. Select Calculate to see the answer and its breakdown.
  3. Keep a scenario, change an input and compare the results.

Use consistent units and check the assumptions below before applying the result.

How probability is calculated

For X~Binomial(n,p), P(X=k)=C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k). Cumulative options sum the relevant outcomes from 0 through n. “At most k” includes zero through k; “at least k” includes k through n. The model describes a fixed number of independent trials with one shared success chance, such as repeated draws with replacement or repeated fair coin flips. With 5 fair coin flips, exactly 2 heads has probability C(5,2)/2⁵=10/32=31.25%.

P(X=k)=C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k), X~Binomial(n,p).
A worked example

With 5 fair coin flips, exactly 2 heads has probability C(5,2)/2⁵=10/32=31.25%.

Assumptions & useful context

The result depends on the values you enter and the method described above. Displayed numbers may be rounded; calculations use the unrounded values. Check that this model matches your situation before relying on it.

Frequently asked questions

What assumptions does the binomial model make?

A fixed trial count, independent trials, and a constant success probability.

Does “at least” include the chosen count?

Yes, it sums k through n.
